issues.legal_issue: A person who had actual or constructive knowledge of an acquisition award cannot obtain a reference by relying on a later notice when the reference application was already outside the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The society objected to the acquisition before the award was made, and its objections were rejected on the ground that it had no right, title, or interest in the land.
The award was made in favour of the recorded landholders, and the society had constructive knowledge of it when it was made.
The society sought a reference years later, relying on a notice subsequently issued to it.
issues.conclusion: The reference application was time-barred, and the Land Acquisition Officer could not validly refer it to the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 12(2) and 18(2) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, limitation runs from actual or constructive knowledge of the award, not necessarily from later formal notice. Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer and Madan v. State of Maharashtra establish that knowledge of the award is essential to commencement of limitation. A party that participated in the acquisition process and knew, or reasonably ought to have known, of the award cannot rely on a later notice to restart limitation.

predicates.acquisition_reference_proceeding: A person sought a judicial reference to challenge or seek reconsideration of compensation awarded in a land acquisition.
predicates.applicant_participated_before_award: The applicant took part in the acquisition process before the award was made.
predicates.applicant_had_constructive_knowledge_of_: The applicant's participation or circumstances meant that a reasonable person in the applicant's position ought to have known of the award when it was made.
predicates.reference_application_was_outside_time_f: The applicant sought a reference after the applicable period had elapsed from the applicant's actual or constructive knowledge of the award.

issues.definition: When a reference applicant participated in the acquisition, ought to have known of the award, and applied after the applicable period from that knowledge, the reference application is time-barred.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee cannot claim acquisition compensation on the basis of a transfer that is void because the landholder belongs to a protected community and the transferee does not.
material_facts: The original landholders belonged to a Scheduled Caste, and that fact was not disputed by the society.
The society relied on alleged agreements to purchase the land from the original landholders, but did not produce the agreements.
The society was a juristic person and did not itself belong to the Scheduled Caste; the civil decrees in its favour were based on the alleged agreements.
The society claimed compensation on the basis of its alleged interest in the land.
issues.conclusion: The alleged transfers were void from their inception, the decrees founded on them were nullities, and the society acquired no right to claim compensation. The original landholders, or their legal representatives, were entitled to the compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act declares void a transfer by a Scheduled Caste landholder to a person outside that community. Read with Article 341 of the Constitution, the statutory reference to a member of a Scheduled Caste means a natural person included in the relevant constitutional notification, not a juristic person. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act cannot protect a claimant under a void transaction. State of Rajasthan v. Aanjaney Organic Herbal Pvt. Ltd. holds that the bar applies to a juristic transferee; Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka supports legislative protection of land held for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Babu Lal and Lincal Gamango v. Dayanidhi Jena address the consequences of prohibited transfers. Ram Karan v. State of Rajasthan also recognises the unlawfulness of a prohibited transfer. The right to compensation rests on a right, title, or interest in the land, which the void transfer did not confer.

rule.if: compensation_entitlement_proceeding and protected_community_landholder and transferee_outside_protected_community and claim_depends_on_prohibited_transfer

predicates.compensation_entitlement_proceeding: A proceeding concerns who is entitled to compensation for acquired land.
predicates.protected_community_landholder: The landholder who transferred or purported to transfer the land belonged to a community protected by restrictions on transfer of the land.
predicates.transferee_outside_protected_community: The purported transferee did not belong to the protected community.
predicates.claim_depends_on_prohibited_transfer: The claimant's asserted interest in the land and claim to compensation depend on the prohibited transfer.

issues.definition: If compensation entitlement depends on a prohibited transfer from a protected-community landholder to a transferee outside that community, only the landholder or a successor may claim the compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to bring ejectment proceedings does not validate a prohibited transfer or prevent a court from examining its validity when compensation entitlement is disputed.
material_facts: The land had already been taken by the acquiring authority before the society obtained civil decrees based on the alleged agreements.
The society argued that the original landholders had lost their remedy because they had not sought ejectment under the tenancy legislation.
The society asserted its entitlement to compensation in proceedings in which the validity of the alleged transfer was in issue.
issues.conclusion: Ejectment proceedings were unnecessary after the acquiring authority had taken possession, and the prohibited transfer could be examined in the compensation proceedings notwithstanding the absence of such proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 175 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act provides for ejectment in cases of illegal transfer, but the court held that ejectment proceedings would have served no purpose once the State had taken possession. The nullity of a transaction under section 42 could be examined in proceedings where a claimant asserted rights based on that transaction. Nathu Ram v. State of Rajasthan and Ram Karan v. State of Rajasthan were considered, but the court distinguished them on the facts, including that possession had already been taken before the later decrees and the asserted compensation entitlement had to be determined in the present proceedings.

predicates.compensation_entitlement_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a claim to compensation arising from acquired land.
predicates.transfer_is_prohibited_and_void: The asserted transfer contravened a restriction that made the transaction void.
predicates.acquiring_authority_already_took_possess: The acquiring authority had taken possession of the land before the claimant relied on the transfer to assert an entitlement.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies on a prohibited, void transfer after the acquiring authority has taken possession, the absence of ejectment proceedings does not validate that transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A direction to allot developed land cannot be based on a policy that applies only to future acquisitions involving surrender of land when the award has already been made and no surrender occurred.
material_facts: The society sought allotment of a share of developed land under a government circular.
The circular applied to future acquisitions in which a landholder surrendered land and contemplated allotment to that landholder, not to another person nominated by the landholder.
The award in these cases had already been made, and the land had not been surrendered under the circular.
The High Court directed consideration of allotment by relying on the circular and an earlier decision based on a concession.
issues.conclusion: The circular did not apply, created no entitlement to allotment in these circumstances, and the High Court's direction to consider allotment of developed land was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of the circular limited its operation to future acquisitions involving surrender of land and excluded allotment to a nominee. The court relied on Jaipur Development Authority v. Vijay Kumar Data and Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam for the limits on acquisition authorities' power to allot acquired land in lieu of compensation, and on the constitutional requirements for formal government action under Article 166. A concession in Smt. Ratni Devi v. State of Rajasthan could not enlarge the circular's scope, and the court would not create negative equality by extending an inapplicable benefit.

rule.if: acquisition_claim_for_developed_land and policy_limited_to_future_surrenders and award_already_made and land_not_surrendered

predicates.acquisition_claim_for_developed_land: A claimant seeks an allotment of developed land as a benefit connected with an acquisition.
predicates.policy_limited_to_future_surrenders: The policy applies only to future acquisitions in which the landholder surrenders the land.
predicates.award_already_made: The acquisition award had been made before the claimant sought the benefit.
predicates.land_not_surrendered: The landholder did not surrender the land under the policy.

issues.definition: Where a claim to developed land relies on a policy limited to future voluntary surrenders, an already-made award and the absence of surrender mean the policy creates no entitlement.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation valuation supported by relevant documentary sale evidence and appropriate deductions need not be increased on the basis of unsupported oral estimates.
material_facts: The Reference Court fixed a higher compensation value after relying on oral estimates of land value.
The High Court considered both oral and documentary evidence, including agreements for sales of comparable land around the relevant period.
The oral estimates lacked a sound evidentiary basis, while the documentary transactions supported a lower average value.
The land acquired was a large area, for which a deduction to account for development requirements was appropriate.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's valuation, based on the documentary evidence and a deduction for the large area acquired, was proper and was upheld; no enhancement was warranted.
issues.legal_principle: The claimant bears the burden of establishing that the awarded compensation should be enhanced. Oral evidence may be considered, but it must be scrutinised and objectively evaluated; unsupported estimates do not prevail over relevant documentary sale evidence. A deduction may be appropriate when a large tract is valued by reference to smaller developed plots. The court applied State of Gujarat v. Rama Rana, Satyanarayana v. Bhu Arjan Adhikari, and Ramanlal Deochand Shah v. State of Maharashtra.

rule.if: compensation_valuation_appeal and relevant_documentary_sale_evidence_exists and oral_estimates_are_unsupported and large_area_requires_development_deduction

predicates.compensation_valuation_appeal: A party appeals the valuation of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.relevant_documentary_sale_evidence_exist: The record contains relevant documentary evidence of land sales that can assist in valuing the acquired land.
predicates.oral_estimates_are_unsupported: Oral estimates of value lack a sound evidentiary basis.
predicates.large_area_requires_development_deductio: The size or undeveloped character of the acquired area makes a deduction for development requirements appropriate.

issues.definition: In a compensation valuation appeal, relevant documentary sales evidence and an appropriate deduction support upholding the valuation when oral estimates are unsupported.

issues.legal_issue: Original landholders whose entitlement to compensation is affected must be heard, and compensation due to protected landholders must be disbursed directly to them or their successors rather than through an intermediary.
material_facts: The society claimed compensation based on the alleged transfer, while the original landholders' entitlement to compensation was directly affected.
The High Court had rejected the original landholders' application to be added as parties.
The original landholders belonged to a Scheduled Caste, and the asserted transfer to the society was void.
The Court determined that the original landholders or their legal representatives were entitled to compensation and directed the acquiring authority to pay them directly.
issues.conclusion: The original landholders were required to be heard in determining entitlement, and the compensation was to be disbursed directly to them or their legal representatives, without payment to the society or another intermediary on their behalf.
issues.legal_principle: Where adjudication determines who is entitled to compensation, persons whose entitlement is directly affected must be heard. In light of the protections for Scheduled Castes and the purpose of section 42 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, payment through an intermediary relying on a void transfer could defeat the landholders' rights. The court relied on the protective constitutional purpose reflected in Article 46 and the constitutional recognition of Scheduled Castes under Article 341.

predicates.compensation_entitlement_proceeding: A proceeding determines who is entitled to compensation for acquired land.
predicates.original_landholders_rights_are_affected: The proceeding may determine whether the persons from whom the land was acquired, or their successors, receive the compensation.
predicates.original_landholders_have_not_been_heard: The original landholders or their successors have not had an opportunity to participate in the determination of entitlement.

issues.definition: When a compensation proceeding may determine the original landholders' entitlement and they have not been heard, they must be heard before that entitlement is resolved.
